idiom_name: package API with exported functions or a coordinator struct; internal/ packages hide the subsystem
implementation_notes: A Go facade is a package: exported identifiers define the surface, unexported types and internal/... packages hold the subsystem, and clients import one path and call a few functions. Use a struct with injected collaborators when the facade needs configuration, mocking or several instances; use package-level functions when there is nothing to inject, accepting that global state makes tests order-dependent. The io package is the standard-library precedent - a small public surface over every Reader/Writer implementation - and internal/ additionally lets the compiler forbid direct use of subsystem packages.
pitfalls: Exporting subsystem types in signatures (or exporting the internal packages) collapses the facade; keep types unexported or define small consumer-side interfaces.
Package-level state (a configured default processor) makes tests order-dependent and hides dependencies; prefer the struct form.
Raw subsystem errors are part of the API: wrap and translate them at the boundary or callers become coupled to implementation details.
A facade package that grows one exported function per subsystem method is a renamed subsystem; keep operations task-shaped.
